South polar skua chicks hatching from eggs incubated under controlled conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] emerge after approximately 29 days [ab = approximately 29 days], a developmental period consistent with the relatively protracted incubation typical of large Stercorariidae. Upon hatching, the mean wet weight at birth is 65 grams [Wwb = 65 grams], a modest mass that belies the rapid growth trajectory these semi-precocial nestlings will undergo during the brief austral summer. This initial body size reflects the considerable yolk reserves invested by the female, which support the chick through its first days of external feeding. Field observations from colonies along the Antarctic coast confirm that hatchlings are brooded intensively for the first week, with parents alternating between incubation of the remaining egg and provisioning of the newly emerged chick. The relatively small hatchling mass compared to the ultimate adult size underscores the dramatic post-natal growth that characterizes this species.

As the chick develops, it attains an ultimate wet weight of 1340 grams [Wwi = 1340 grams] by the time it reaches adult stature, representing a more than twenty-fold increase from its neonatal mass. This substantial gain in body mass is fueled by a diet dominated by fish, krill, and occasionally the eggs and chicks of other seabirds, which parents deliver with remarkable regularity to the nest. Adult body mass shows some seasonal variation, with individuals at the end of the breeding season typically weighing slightly less due to the energetic demands of chick-rearing, but the asymptotic mass of approximately 1340 grams emerges as a reliable benchmark for fully grown, healthy adults. This value positions the South polar skua as a moderately large member of its genus, comparable in size to the brown skua but distinguished by its slightly more gracile build and lighter plumage. Males and females exhibit no pronounced sexual dimorphism in mass, though females tend to be marginally heavier on average during the pre-laying period.

This milestone marks the point at which the developing chick achieves sufficient flight feather maturation and muscle development to sustain its first sustained flights, though parental provisioning often continues for several additional weeks as the fledgling refines its foraging skills. The timing of fledging is critically linked to the brevity of the Antarctic summer; chicks that fledge too late risk insufficient time to build adequate fat reserves before the onset of winter. Nest departure at 49 days after hatching thus represents a finely tuned balance between the need for sufficient growth and the imperative to complete development before environmental conditions deteriorate. The post-fledging period is characterized by a gradual transition to nutritional independence, with young birds increasingly accompanying their parents on foraging trips.

Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity to produce gametes, is reached at 147 days after hatching [tp = 147 days after hatching] when individuals are metabolically active at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This relatively rapid progression to sexual competence is notable among large seabirds, many of which defer maturation for several years. However, although the physiological machinery for reproduction is in place by roughly five months of age, South polar skuas typically do not engage in breeding until considerably later, as they must first establish territories and accumulate the experience necessary to successfully rear offspring. The attainment of puberty at 147 days after hatching thus represents the earliest possible point at which an individual could theoretically contribute gametes, but social and ecological constraints ordinarily delay actual reproductive engagement. This decoupling of physiological from social maturity is a common life-history strategy among long-lived, territorial seabirds.

First breeding in the South polar skua occurs at approximately 5 years after hatching [tR = approximately 5 years after hatching], which represents the time since birth at first brood when measured at the species active body temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This delay between the attainment of puberty and the onset of actual reproduction reflects the considerable investment required to acquire and defend a high-quality nesting territory within the competitive colonial environment. Maximum recorded longevity in the wild is 23.5 years [am = 23.5 years] for individuals operating at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], a lifespan that enables multiple reproductive opportunities over a protracted adult phase. Reproductive output is modest, with females typically producing 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch] and raising 1 brood per year [F_R_i = 1 brood per year], a conservative strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity in the harsh polar environment. This combination of delayed maturity, extended lifespan, and low annual fecundity aligns with the classic slow life-history pace observed in many long-lived seabird species adapted to resource-poor, high-latitude ecosystems.
